title: Harnesses · Orchestration
description: Trace how a harness executes and records model-selected actions, then follow a task outward into scheduling, identity, recovery and publication.

blocks.body:
Take the file-read request from the previous chapter and send exactly the same request to two systems. Both use the same model and both accept the path `src/retry.js`. One reads the file in the current checkout. The other reads a stale checkout left behind by yesterday's job.

The request is identical, the path is valid, and both tools can truthfully report that a read succeeded. Yet the model is now reasoning about two different programs. If the second investigation goes wrong, changing the model is unlikely to address the cause. We need to inspect the machinery that gave the request its meaning.

That machinery is the **harness**. In this course, the term covers the runtime around the model: assembling inputs, interpreting requests, managing access to tools, collecting observations and maintaining the state of a run. A product may spread those responsibilities across several services. The term names the job they collectively perform, not a requirement that they live in one library.

A useful way to picture the harness is as the set of connections in our feedback diagram. It decides which environment an action reaches, what actually runs there, and which account of the result returns. Those connections determine whether the model's decisions stay attached to the world it is supposed to be changing.

sections.title: Follow a read all the way back

blocks.body:
Suppose a model asks to read the retry implementation. First, the runtime identifies the requested tool and interprets the arguments. A malformed request is a failure at this interface; no file has been read. A well-formed request can move to the next boundary: is this operation permitted in the assigned workspace?

A file path is relative to something. The harness needs a defined workspace and a policy for resolving the requested path within it. A path that looks harmless as a string may resolve somewhere else through a symbolic link. An allowed file tool also provides little isolation if another exposed tool gives unrestricted shell access to the same machine. The effective boundary comes from the combination of the tool implementation and the execution environment.

After the read runs, its result needs to stay associated with the request that produced it. Imagine two reads in flight: the implementation and its test. If the responses are attached to the wrong calls, the bytes may be accurate while the resulting conversation is misleading. Request identities and explicit result types let the runtime preserve those associations without asking the model to guess.

The final step is easy to overlook: the next model input must include the useful observation. Logging the file contents somewhere is not sufficient. The runtime may keep the full artifact outside the input and supply an excerpt, but then the excerpt needs enough context and a retrieval path to the rest. We will examine that selection problem in chapter three.

Here is a small fictional trace. It records the externally observable sequence, not a transcript of the model's private reasoning:

```text
run: retry-17    checkout: a17c9e    workspace: /work/retry-17
call-08 requested  read_file("src/retry.js")
call-08 permitted workspace read
call-08 returned  source bytes from /work/retry-17/src/retry.js
turn-09 includes  call-08 result
```

If the agent later says it could not find the function, this trace gives us a starting point. Did the tool return the wrong revision? Was the relevant part truncated? Was the result omitted from turn 09? Or was the right evidence present and misinterpreted? These possibilities require different repairs. The harness makes them distinguishable by recording what crossed each boundary.

blocks.question: The read tool returned the correct source, but the next model input contains only “file read successfully”. Where did the investigation lose the evidence?
blocks.answer: Between execution and context assembly. The filesystem operation worked, but the runtime replaced its useful observation with a status message. The next call cannot inspect bytes it was never given. Check what was actually supplied to that call, rather than rerunning the read or changing the model first.

sections.title: Failure needs enough shape to guide recovery

blocks.body:
Now replace the file read with a request to run the focused retry test. The command can fail before the test runner starts, while dependencies load, or at the assertion we care about. It can also run the wrong test suite successfully. Compressing all of this into a boolean discards the distinctions that determine the next useful move.

Suppose the same investigation works on a developer's machine but fails in CI. The local command ran from the package directory; the CI command ran one directory above it. “Test failed” invites the model to alter the implementation. “No package configuration found in this working directory” points to the environment. The observation should make the second explanation available before anyone starts repairing code that has not been exercised.

A good tool interface preserves the command's meaning: working directory, exit status, relevant output, whether it timed out, and whether it ran at all. It can distinguish a rejected request from an executed request that failed. The precise schema varies with the tool, but its categories should help the caller choose between correcting arguments, seeking missing setup, inspecting application behaviour and stopping with a blocker.

Prompts still matter here. Tool descriptions can explain what an argument means and how to interpret a result. But an instruction to stay inside a workspace influences a choice; executable permissions constrain what the chosen operation can do. The two support one another. Neither an excellent description nor a strict permission boundary ensures that the model chose a useful experiment.

sections.title: The awkward case: did the action happen?

blocks.body:
A read is a comfortable example because repeating it usually leaves the world unchanged. Consider an action that creates a tracking issue. The request reaches the service, the service creates the issue, and then the connection breaks before the confirmation arrives. From the caller's perspective, the action timed out.

Should the harness try again? It cannot infer from the timeout alone that nothing happened. Repeating the request may create a duplicate. This is a distributed-systems problem inside an agent workflow: the state of the world and the caller's knowledge of that state have diverged.

When an operation supports an idempotency key, repeated delivery of the same logical request can be recognised as one operation. When it does not, the system may need to look up the external result or report that the outcome is uncertain. A file-editing tool has a related problem: if its confirmation is lost, inspecting the current file may be safer than blindly applying the same edit again. The recovery policy depends on the operation's effects.

Even a test result has a time boundary. Suppose the agent runs the right tests on a patch, then makes one last edit to tidy the implementation. The previous test result remains a real observation, but it describes the earlier workspace. We can no longer attach it to the final diff without checking whether the intervening edit invalidates it. A commit ID alone also misses uncommitted changes; the relevant identity is the actual workspace state that was tested.

This is why a harness needs more than a loop counter. It manages outstanding operations, cancellation, resource limits and enough state to explain what is known when a run stops. A cancelled command may have produced partial effects. A completed tool call may still have an ambiguous application outcome. The final report should preserve these distinctions instead of converting every interruption into “failed” or every normal return into “done”.

blocks.question: A report-creation call times out. What evidence would make a retry reasonable?
blocks.answer: You need to know how the operation handles repeated delivery. A supported idempotency key may make the same request safe to resend. Otherwise inspect the external system for the original result, or preserve the uncertainty for review. The timeout alone does not establish whether the report was created.

blocks.body:
So far, somebody has already given our harness an investigation to perform. Now imagine the full repository service. A CI failure arrives, a job is created, an isolated checkout is prepared, and the agent investigates. Later, a person or a constrained publishing stage decides what to do with the result.

Those surrounding decisions are **orchestration**: choosing when work starts, which task and environment a run receives, how runs are identified, and where their results go. The harness manages operations within a run; the outer workflow manages the run's place in a larger process. A single product can implement both. Keeping the responsibilities separate helps us reason about failures without depending on product names.

Watch what happens when a new commit arrives during the investigation. The agent may produce a perfectly sound diagnosis of the old commit. The workflow still needs to decide whether that result is relevant to the latest one. Rerunning the model with stronger instructions cannot make an old test result describe new code. The task and result need an identity that the outer system can compare with the current repository state.

Now deliver the same failure event twice. Should it start two investigations? Perhaps one is already running; perhaps the second event contains new evidence. The workflow needs a definition of the logical job and a policy for duplicate or superseded work. This is a different identity problem from matching a tool result to its request, but the reason is familiar: an observation only helps when we know what it describes.

data.title: One investigation sits inside a larger lifecycle
data.caption: The outer workflow assigns a revision and eventually decides whether the result still applies. Inside it, the harness runs the model–tool feedback loop. A successful investigation can still be obsolete by the time it returns.

blocks.body:
A schedule simply gives this process a repeatable trigger. It does not supply the missing judgment about when a result is useful. A nightly investigator should be able to return “no new actionable finding” without inventing an issue to demonstrate activity. It should also be able to distinguish that outcome from “could not inspect the failing run”. Silence after a successful check and silence after a broken job have very different meanings.

We can now locate three operating modes. With assistance, a person steers as the work proceeds. With delegation, the person hands over a bounded task and returns to inspect its result. With automation, an event or schedule can initiate that delegation under an established policy. Each can use the same inner agent loop. Automation increases how often and how independently the process runs; any weaknesses in its investigation and reporting go with it.

sections.title: Build around the requirement you actually have

blocks.body:
These responsibilities can make a custom harness look attractive. Yet many failures we have just discussed can be fixed by configuring an existing system: setting its working directory, giving it a suitable tool, preserving a result or narrowing permissions. Owning a replacement also means owning provider changes, tool schemas, recovery, cancellation and the unremarkable cases where nothing useful should happen.

A concrete missing requirement is a stronger reason to build. Suppose every write must pass through a transaction service that records an application-specific audit event, and the available runtime cannot route writes that way. Then a custom integration may have a clear purpose. The decision can be discussed in terms of the boundary it enables and the operational cost of keeping that boundary correct.

Before scheduling our retry investigator, we can try it manually on a known failing run, a run with broken setup, and a run whose problem is already fixed. If it cannot distinguish those cases under observation, removing the observer will not supply the missing distinction. The design is ready to become more independent when we can explain both its useful results and its ordinary reasons to do nothing.

data.title: Lab 1 · Follow one failure through the system
data.brief: Sketch a service that investigates a failed retry test and recommends a next action. Use paper or a document; no model account is needed. Develop the design by changing what happens around one run.
steps: Begin with the failed CI run and its revision. Draw how an investigation receives the code, requests a test and returns its evidence.
Erase the path that returns the test output to the next model call. Explain what the model can still do and what it has lost. Restore the missing handoff.
Deliver the original event a second time, then introduce a newer commit while the first investigation is running. Decide which results may still be used and where that decision belongs.
Let publication time out after possibly succeeding. Show how your design discovers the outcome or reports uncertainty without blindly publishing again.
deliverables: An annotated drawing showing the inner loop and the outer lifecycle
Notes explaining how the design responds to missing feedback, duplicate work and an uncertain publication
data.review: Follow the drawing as if you were each component. The model should receive observations before making decisions that depend on them. The harness should know which operation produced each result. The outer workflow should know which task and revision the result concerns. If your publication service cannot safely deduplicate a retry, an explicit uncertain outcome is more defensible than an automatic second write. Different designs can meet these requirements; the point is to make each consequence explainable.

blocks.body: The drawing still has one deceptively small box: the input for the next model call. A harness might transport every result correctly and still give the model a confusing account of the investigation. The next chapter asks how to choose and organise that account, and how to keep it useful when a conversation grows or a new session takes over.

heading: What makes a sensible action turn into dependable work?
lead: Open up the machinery around the model. A file path, a tool result and a successful test all get their meaning from an execution context—and a useful agent system has to keep that context intact.
outcomes: Trace a request through validation, execution, observation and the next model call.
Explain why timeouts, permissions and changing workspaces require explicit handling.
Separate the lifecycle of one agent run from the workflow that starts and uses it.
